% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 1--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
Type violations are ontologically invalid regardless of downstream application: a triple whose head or tail type lies outside the relation's domain/range specification contradicts the schema definition.
At deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%), where extracted triples feed directly into knowledge graphs, reliable type-safety enforcement is needed.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains, but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it discards the majority of outputs and becomes impractical.
OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation rather than discarding non-compliant outputs.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} provide only soft guidance that cannot eliminate violations.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that compiles an IE schema into two composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
Our two-layer architecture reflects the observation that structural violations (malformed output, unknown types) and semantic violations (type-constraint breaches) require fundamentally different enforcement mechanisms.
The \emph{grammar layer} enforces JSON well-formedness and vocabulary validity via XGrammar.
The \emph{semantic layer} maintains a stateful entity registry during generation: as entities are decoded, the registry records type assignments; when relation arguments are generated, dynamic logit masking restricts output to types compatible with the relation's domain/range specification.
The layers compose via bitwise AND with an \emph{enabling dependency}: the grammar layer guarantees vocabulary membership, so the semantic layer can look up domain/range rules.
Unlike type-constrained code generation where types are statically declared, IE requires a dynamic entity registry built during generation, with constraint targets that depend on the co-occurring relation.
OntoCoDec requires no constraint-specific training; it composes with standard LoRA fine-tuning that targets the base model's IE ability, and applies to any autoregressive LM.
We evaluate two deployment configurations: LoRA + greedy S1 eliminates DR with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp and $+$10\% latency; LoRA + beam S1 ($k{=}4$) additionally resolves the CF trade-off, achieving zero violations on SciERC (1.54$\times$ latency).
Zero-shot evaluation across four models (8B--70B) confirms DR drops by 76--99\% for calibrated models.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item An empirical characterization of type violations in LLM-based IE, identifying four violation categories (DR, RV, ET, CF) and their correlation with schema constraint tightness across 103 relations.
    \item OntoCoDec, a two-layer framework compiling IE schemas into stateful logit masks that enforce pair-based domain/range constraints during autoregressive IE, unlike code generation where types are statically declared.
    \item Two deployment configurations: (1)~LoRA + greedy S1 achieves DR$\to$0\% with R-F1 $\pm$0.6\,pp and CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\% ($+$10\% latency); (2)~LoRA + beam S1 ($k{=}4$) eliminates all four violation types on SciERC (1.54$\times$ latency). Zero-shot evaluation across four models (8B--70B) confirms DR reductions of 76--99\% for calibrated models. The framework extends to event extraction without modification (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}, preliminary, 20-document test set).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

We provide a detailed survey in Appendix~\ref{app:related_work}; here we position OntoCoDec along three axes.

\paragraph{Grammar-constrained decoding.}
XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}, Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines}, LMQL~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql}, SynCode~\cite{ugare2024syncode}, and Grammar-Aligned Decoding~\cite{park2024grammar} guarantee format validity via CFG-based token masking; JSONSchemaBench~\cite{jsonschemabench2025} benchmarks these systems.
GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd} applies grammar constraints to IE tasks.
In code generation, PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} and Synchromesh~\cite{synchromesh_iclr2022} enforce type constraints via incremental parsing, and \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compile full type systems into prefix automata.
These methods ensure syntactic or type-level validity but operate on static type declarations; IE requires a dynamic entity registry built during generation, where constraint targets depend on the co-occurring relation type.
OntoCoDec's grammar layer builds on XGrammar; its semantic layer extends constrained decoding from syntax to ontology-level type enforcement.

\paragraph{Schema-aware IE.}
GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie}, GUIDEX~\cite{guidex2025}, and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024} encode ontology structure as Python dataclasses and train models to generate typed code;
REBEL~\cite{cabot2021rebel}, InstructUIE~\cite{wang2023instructuie}, DeepStruct~\cite{wang2022deepstruct}, UIE~\cite{lu2022uie}, USM~\cite{lou2023usm}, and UniversalNER~\cite{zhou2024universalner} unify extraction via structured training, though schema compliance gaps persist~\cite{wadhwa2023revisiting}.
These methods internalize constraints through training; code-generation approaches such as GoLLIE achieve type compliance through format constraints (class names encode types) but with limited zero-shot relation coverage.
OntoCoDec enforces types at decoding time without retraining while preserving extraction capability.

\paragraph{Constraint enforcement in IE.}
\citet{roth_yih_2004} first formulated hard type constraints for IE via integer linear programming; OntoCoDec achieves analogous enforcement within autoregressive decoding.
Post-hoc validation~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025,slot2025} detects violations after generation and requires rejection or correction cycles.
EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} enforces structural constraints via ASP but requires hand-crafted rules; IterGen~\cite{ugare2025itergen} supports semantic constraints via backtracking but requires manual implementation per constraint.
BoostCD~\cite{boostcd2025} combines constrained and unconstrained decoding for IE; SchemaRL~\cite{schema_rl2025} uses reinforcement learning to align generation with schema constraints; DCCD~\cite{dccd2026} accelerates constrained decoding via draft-conditioned generation.
Recent work shows constrained decoding can degrade reasoning~\cite{banerjee2025crane,schall2025hiddencost,formattax2026}; however, extraction tasks are robust to format constraints~\cite{tam2024letmespeak}, and OntoCoDec constrains only type tokens while leaving entity spans unconstrained.
OntoCoDec prevents violations during decoding, requires no constraint-specific training, and compiles constraints automatically from IE schemas.

8	\paragraph{Implementation challenges.}
9	Two stateful components require adaptation for beam search.
10	(1)~The grammar layer (XGrammar) maintains an internal \texttt{GrammarMatcher} state that tracks the generated token sequence; beam reordering invalidates this state because beams are permuted across steps.
11	Our solution instantiates a fresh \texttt{GrammarMatcher} per beam per step and replays the beam's current token sequence through XGrammar's stateless accept API (64 lines of code).
12	(2)~The semantic layer's \texttt{TypeConstraintProcessor} accumulates entity and relation registries that assume a single generation path.
13	Our solution isolates state per beam by calling \texttt{detect()} on the full partial output at each step, reconstructing all entity/relation state from scratch for each beam independently (61 lines of code).
14	Both adaptations add ${\sim}125$ lines total without modifying the existing greedy/sampling logic.
15	
16	\paragraph{Results.}
17	Table~\ref{tab:beam-search} compares beam search ($k{=}4$, \texttt{early\_stopping=True}) against greedy decoding under full S1 constraints across six model-dataset combinations.

101	With DR=0 in 50 DocRED documents for both calibrated models, the Clopper-Pearson 95\% CI upper bound is 5.8\%, so the zero-DR result is statistically meaningful despite the limited sample.
102	Combined with the sampling robustness results (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling}), these findings confirm that OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is compatible with greedy, sampling, and beam search decoding without modification to the core constraint logic.

Our solution isolates state per beam by calling \texttt{detect()} on the full partial output at each step, reconstructing all entity/relation state from scratch for each beam independently (61 lines of code).
Both adaptations add ${\sim}125$ lines total without modifying the existing greedy/sampling logic.

\paragraph{Results.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-search} compares beam search ($k{=}4$, \texttt{early\_stopping=True}) against greedy decoding under full S1 constraints across six model-dataset combinations.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Beam search ($k{=}4$) vs.\ greedy decoding under full S1 constraints.

\toprule
\textbf{Model / Dataset} & \textbf{Decoding} & ET & RV & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\

  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.55} & 58.64 & 9.37 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B / SciERC (551)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.08 & 6.56 & 23.49 & 2.54 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.93} & 25.04 & 3.33 \\
\midrule

\paragraph{Discussion.}
For calibrated models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), beam search achieves DR=0\% across all four model-dataset combinations (both SciERC with 7 entity types, 551 documents, and DocRED with 96 relation types, 50 documents), regardless of schema complexity.
On SciERC, beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (0.93\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (0.08\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and substantially reduces CF (Qwen: 9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.53\%; Llama: 6.56\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
On DocRED (matched 50-document subsets), beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (8.69\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (1.58\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with CF reductions of 74\% and 86\% respectively.
Llama DocRED shows the largest R-F1 gain ($+$3.4\,pp), consistent with beam search recovering valid type assignments that greedy decoding missed due to constraint fallback.
The CF reduction is an indirect effect: beam search reduces constraint-fallback frequency by exploring alternative token sequences that satisfy both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously, avoiding the fallback-to-grammar path that produces cross-field inconsistencies under greedy decoding.

Mistral-7B-v0.3 constitutes a boundary condition on both datasets.
On SciERC (7 entity types), beam search does not reduce DR (13.4\%\,$\to$\,13.8\%), though CF drops by 55\% relative (1.27\%\,$\to$\,0.57\%) and R-F1 improves by $+$0.7\,pp; the unchanged DR confirms that all residual violations stem from entity type misclassification, not constraint-search failure.
On DocRED (96 relation types), beam search reduces DR by 25\% relative (28.4\%\,$\to$\,21.4\%): the more complex schema introduces constraint-search failures that beam exploration resolves, but the entity misclassification component remains.
This contrast reveals that beam search resolves constraint-search failure (where greedy decoding encounters $G(t) \cap S(t) = \emptyset$ conflicts) but cannot overcome fundamental model calibration limitations in entity typing.

\paragraph{Beam width ablation.}

DR elimination at $k{\geq}4$ confirms that constraint-search failure is resolved with moderate exploration width.
CF continues to decrease with larger beam (0.08\% at $k{=}8$, only 2 residual violations), while entity extraction quality improves monotonically.
$k{=}4$ represents the optimal cost-effectiveness trade-off: it eliminates all DR violations at roughly half the compute cost of $k{=}8$.

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
Under greedy decoding, the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B (LoRA, SciERC) with full S1 constraints already achieves DR=0\% but retains CF=1.18\% (21 cross-field violations across 551 documents), with E-F1=67.05 and R-F1=43.77.
Adding beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all residual CF violations (1.18\%\,$\to$\,0\%), yielding zero violations across all four metrics (ET=0\%, RV=0\%, DR=0\%, CF=0\%) while preserving extraction quality (E-F1=66.88, R-F1=44.23; changes within $\pm$0.5\,pp).
Llama-3.1-8B (LoRA, SciERC) with full S1 constraints and beam search ($k{=}4$) likewise achieves zero violations across all four metrics (ET=0\%, RV=0\%, DR=0\%, CF=0\%) with R-F1=46.11; the zero-violation result thus generalizes across calibrated model families.

The three constraint mechanisms (grammar masking, semantic domain-range filtering, and beam exploration) are thus fully composable: each addresses a distinct violation source without interfering with the others or degrading task performance.

Beam search on DocRED introduces a modest increase in parse failures (3/50, 6\%) compared to greedy (1.1\%), as longer beam-generated sequences occasionally produce malformed JSON in complex documents.
With DR=0 in 50 DocRED documents for both calibrated models, the Clopper-Pearson 95\% CI upper bound is 5.8\%, so the zero-DR result is statistically meaningful despite the limited sample.
Combined with the sampling robustness results (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling}), these findings confirm that OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is compatible with greedy, sampling, and beam search decoding without modification to the core constraint logic.

\paragraph{Latency overhead.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-latency} reports wall-clock latency for greedy and beam search ($k{=}4$) under LoRA fine-tuning.

\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{s/doc} & \textbf{Overhead} \\

\end{tabular}
\caption{Latency per document (SciERC, 551 docs, Qwen3-8B LoRA FT, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell). Overhead relative to greedy unconstrained.}
\label{tab:beam-latency}
\end{table}

Beam search itself adds 32\% latency (4 beams); constraint overhead increases from 10\% (greedy) to 16.5\% (beam) because each beam independently maintains grammar and semantic state.
The total 1.54$\times$ overhead is acceptable for offline batch IE; \texttt{early\_stopping} limits additional compute to partial-sequence exploration.

We also explored a type-consensus constraint that forces identical entity types across all relations within a document.
However, CF violations occur precisely where the consensus type conflicts with domain-range constraints, creating a fundamental CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off.
With DR-aware enforcement (skipping consensus when it would violate domain-range), the layer becomes a no-op (100\% skip rate on 551 SciERC documents and 50 DocRED documents).
This confirms that beam search resolves the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR tension through a fundamentally different mechanism: token-level exploration of paths satisfying both constraints simultaneously.

3	At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
4	The final mask is their conjunction:
5	%
6	\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
7	  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
8	\end{equation}
9	%
10	so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
11	The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$. This reflects the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.
12	
13	\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
14	When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
15	We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
16	Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.
17	Among type violations, DR and CF differ in severity: a DR violation renders the triple ontologically invalid (the entity type lies outside the relation's domain or range), whereas a CF violation means each triple is individually schema-valid but the same entity receives different type assignments across triples.
18	
19	\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
20	Recall the tightness of relation $r$ (\S\ref{sec:bg:ontology}):\footnote{For symmetric relations, $|\sigma(r)|$ counts ordered pairs; the normalization $|\mathcal{E}|^2$ remains appropriate since we evaluate on directed triples.}
21	%
22	\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
23	  \kappa(r) = 1 - \frac{|\sigma(r)|}{|\mathcal{E}|^2},
24	\end{equation}
25	%
26	The mean tightness $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$ characterizes schema restrictiveness.
27	Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions; fallback frequency and residual DR increase accordingly.
28	This dual-factor pattern (tightness $\times$ baseline violation rate) is consistent with the cross-dataset results: SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction vs.\ DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$) at 45--90\%; the full range across three models is 42--99\% (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}; Appendix~\ref{app:dual-factor}).
29	The pattern extends to WikiEvents EE ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.82$; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents-kappa}).
